content: The provision of clean cooking technologies and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) has been supported through collaborative efforts involving the public sector, producers, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs). Numerous examples exist where such partnerships have successfully promoted the development and adoption of improved stoves and cleaner fuels. In the United Republic of Tanzania, accredited drug dispensing outlets (ADDOs), also known as Duka la Dawa Muhimu or Duka la Dawa Baridi, are authorized to provide non-prescription medicines to the private sector. With over 4,600 stores, ADDOs represent the largest network of licensed retail outlets for purchasing medicines in the country. The ADDO initiative was designed to enhance access to affordable, high-quality medicines and pharmaceutical services in rural and peri-urban areas where registered pharmacies are scarce or nonexistent. To achieve this, the Strategies for Enhancing Access to Medicines (SEAM) Program adopted a comprehensive approach. This included efforts to change the behaviors and expectations of individuals and groups involved in retail drug shops, such as shop owners, dispensing staff, regulators, and clients. For shop owners and staff, the program combined training, incentives, consumer pressure, and regulatory enforcement. Simultaneously, it worked to influence client demand for and expectations of quality products and services. An evaluation of ADDO shops in 2004 compared them to a control group of non-accredited drug outlets. Key lessons learned included the following: Pharmaceutical services in developing countries can be significantly improved through training, accreditation, and regulation of private-sector drug sellers, but supervision and monitoring are essential. Broad-based support from stakeholders in both the public and private sectors is critical for the successful design and implementation of such projects. Defining the appropriate mix of publicand private-sector responsibilities tailored to the country’s context is crucial for timely scaling and sustainability. Training for shop owners, dispensers, and local regulators, as well as supervision and mentoring, is resource-intensive and must be adequately addressed in sustainability and rollout strategies. In Uttar Pradesh, India, the Point-of-Use Water Disinfection and Zinc Treatment (POUZN) Project aimed to improve the quality of care for childhood diarrhea by introducing zinc and oral rehydration salts (ORS). Recognizing that public health sector distribution alone would not reach the most vulnerable populations, the project collaborated with commercial partners to produce and sell zinc. However, informal practitioners and retail outlets in remote areas were not directly engaged. To address this gap, the project trained approximately 2,000 rural medical practitioners (RMPs) and 500 drug sellers through local NGOs to provide access to zinc and ORS in underserved areas. These unlicensed providers typically treat around 63% of children under three years old suffering from diarrhea. The project also developed communication tools, such as a short DVD, to raise awareness and ensure consistent messaging about zinc. Retailers were provided with DVD players and simple monitoring forms to track prescription practices and client satisfaction. Following a review, the strategy was refined, and the program expanded to cover a catchment area of approximately 13 million people, involving 20,000 RMPs and 5,000 drug sellers. This approach led to significant increases in the use of recommended point-of-use water treatment and improved access to zinc and other health products in rural markets. In Ethiopia, the Last Ten Kilometres (L10K) Project implemented a community-based strategy called Participatory Community Quality Improvement (PCQI) to enhance the quality and accessibility of healthcare services. This approach involved community members identifying barriers to service access and quality, proposing solutions, and taking responsibility for monitoring improvements. Health Extension Workers (HEWs) also participated in quarterly meetings to address these issues. Positive changes observed within a year included addressing harmful traditional beliefs, improving access to services, and enhancing HEWs’ practical experience. Community-driven initiatives included maintaining roads to clinics, constructing HEW lodgings near health facilities for emergency services, and pooling funds to purchase supplies for health posts. Globally, progress in child survival depends on delivering high-quality, adequately funded interventions. Monitoring service quality is essential for program management, and tools and guidelines exist to measure both the content and process of quality improvement efforts. WHO and partners have developed facility-level quality indicators for maternal, neonatal, and child health services, which are intended for routine assessment and application to improve services. Methods to assess community-level child health care quality have also been developed and used in countries like Ethiopia and Malawi. Sustainability of health interventions is critical, especially as external funding diminishes or priorities shift. Efforts to sustain improvements in pneumonia and diarrhea interventions should focus on maintaining gains achieved. Monitoring and evaluation are essential to track progress, with countries responsible for ensuring data availability and use. Indicators for the Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhea (GAPPD) have been aligned with Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and other global initiatives. WHO and UNICEF have been leading efforts to develop post-2015 water and sanitation targets, with specific indicators adapted to the GAPPD timeline. In summary, collaborative efforts, community engagement, and evidence-based strategies are essential for improving access to quality healthcare, sustaining interventions, and achieving global health goals.
